stacks.name: Static HTML
stacks.summary: The reference page with no JavaScript at all. Every interaction is a full page load: forms post and links navigate. It shows what the network and the server cost on their own.

stacks.name: Vanilla JS
stacks.summary: The reference page plus one small, hand-written module: event delegation, fetch and DOM updates, no library. It stands for the least JavaScript these interactions need.

idioms.choice: The module loads in <head> as type=module, so it runs after parsing without blocking it.
Search and category filters hide and show the cards the server rendered; the quick view fetches the product's details as JSON when opened.

stacks.name: Alpine.js
stacks.summary: The reference page with Alpine's directives written into the server's markup. One module, Alpine bundled with the page's stores and components, loads up front and starts Alpine over the server-rendered HTML; stores hold the cart and the filters, and the cart, the quick view and the newsletter call the shared JSON API.

idioms.choice: Alpine is installed from npm and imported into the page's bundle ("As a module", which the installation guide calls the more robust approach) rather than loaded as the script-tag build: the page has its own stores and components, and its code imports the scenario's helpers, so it needs a build step anyway. Everything is registered between importing Alpine and the single Alpine.start() call, as the guide requires, and window.Alpine is set as in the guide's snippet.

Alpine leaves the bundler open. Vite bundles and minifies Alpine with the page's code into one module, and the Node server writes its <script type="module"> tag into <head> from Vite's manifest, as Vite's backend integration describes. A module script is deferred, like the defer attribute that the script-tag installation asks for.

Vite's modulepreload polyfill is turned off (build.modulePreload.polyfill: false), the alternative the backend integration guide gives to importing it: the build is one chunk, and the page has no <link rel="modulepreload"> for it to handle.

The page is the app's own server template (page.js), rendered per request by the scenario's small Node page server, which also takes the form posts made without JavaScript. It copies the reference markup, ids and text, and writes Alpine's directives into it. The reference render has no attribute hooks on the product cards (x-show), the result count and the newsletter status (x-text) or the dialog's contents, so the app does not use it.

The cart and the filters, which several parts of the page share, are global stores (Alpine.store) registered from the bundle before Alpine.start(). They start from JSON that the server renders into the page (the cart it read from the cookie, the category, and the products it rendered a card for), so every binding starts on the text the server rendered.

Parts of the page that only read or change store state (the header's cart line, the search form, the category links, the result count and the product list) are data-less components, each with a bare x-data, rather than one component around the whole page.

The newsletter form and the quick view dialog are components registered with Alpine.data from the bundle. The server passes their starting state as initial parameters (x-data="newsletter(...)"), written as JSON and escaped for the attribute.

Search and category filters run in the browser over the cards the server rendered, like the docs' search input: the search box is bound to the filters store with x-model, each card has x-show, and the result count is a getter. Nothing is fetched, so there is no debounce and results change on every key.

The search box uses x-model.fill, so the query starts from the box's value: the one the server rendered, or what someone typed before the script arrived, which plain x-model would overwrite with the store's value.

Cards that the server filters out carry style="display: none" instead of the reference's hidden attribute, because x-show hides and shows with the inline display property and leaves the attribute alone.

No x-cloak: the server renders every element in the state that Alpine starts from, so nothing flickers while Alpine loads. x-cloak would also need an [x-cloak] rule, which the shared stylesheet does not have.
Forms and links keep their action and href, so the page works without JavaScript and before Alpine starts; Alpine takes them over with @submit.prevent and @click.prevent.
Add to cart, the quick view and the newsletter call the shared JSON API with fetch, from async store and component methods.

A card's Quick view link dispatches a quick-view event with $dispatch; the dialog component listens with @quick-view.window, fetches the product, sets it for its x-text bindings and opens with showModal(). It opens right after the product is set, without $nextTick: Alpine applies the bindings in a microtask, before the next frame is painted, so the dialog never shows the previous product.
The newsletter component reads the address through x-ref when the form is sent, rather than binding it with x-model, since nothing else needs it.

stacks.name: Angular
stacks.summary: The page rendered per request by @angular/ssr's Express server and hydrated with Angular 22's defaults: incremental hydration, with the newsletter below the fold hydrating when it scrolls into view, and event replay. httpResource reads the shared JSON API, whose answers on the server reach the browser in the transfer cache; search and category are query parameters filtered in the browser, and the forms post to Express without JavaScript and to the API once hydrated.

idioms.choice: The project is laid out the way `ng new --ssr` writes it with Angular CLI 22.2: standalone components with the 2025 file names, the application builder, zoneless change detection and OnPush components (both defaults in 22), src/server.ts and the app's server config. The template's placeholder page, favicon, global styles.css and test setup are left out.

`ng build` (outputMode server) builds the browser bundles and the Node server, and `npm run serve:ssr:wirestore`, the script `ng new --ssr` adds, runs node dist/wirestore/server/server.mjs: the template's Express server with AngularNodeAppEngine, which reads $PORT. It also takes $HOST (127.0.0.1), where the template listens on every interface.

One server route, `**` with RenderMode.Server, so every request is rendered on the server: the header shows the visitor's cart, from a cookie. The template's default is RenderMode.Prerender; nothing is prerendered.

Hydration is provideClientHydration() with its defaults, as the template writes it. In Angular 22 they include incremental hydration and, with it, event replay: withIncrementalHydration() is deprecated because it is now the default, so it is not added.

The newsletter, below the 50 cards, is a @defer block with `hydrate on viewport`: the server renders it, and its component's code, a separate chunk, loads and hydrates when it scrolls into view. Until then its form posts without JavaScript. `on viewport` and a @placeholder cover client-side rendering, which this page never does, as the guide asks.

The rest of the page hydrates at once: the header, the search, the categories and the cards respond as soon as the filters or the cart change, and a card left dehydrated until interaction would have its first "Add to cart" posted by the browser, since event replay queues a submit without preventing its default action.

Listeners on forms and links return early when the browser has already acted. Event replay calls, after hydration, the listeners of events from before it, marked `event.eventPhase === EventPhase.REPLAY` (the check Angular's replay error points to, since preventDefault() then throws), and incremental hydration calls those of a @defer block once it has hydrated. Such a form was posted by the browser, so sending it again would add to the cart twice.

Add to cart and the newsletter are plain forms (method=post, action /cart and /newsletter) with a (submit) listener, in an attribute directive for add to cart. Angular's form directives are not used, since they would handle a form the browser has already sent: Signal Forms' FormRoot calls preventDefault() on every submit, which throws during event replay, and adds novalidate.

Without JavaScript the forms reach two Express routes in src/server.ts, before the Angular handler, where the template puts API endpoints: they update the cart cookie with the scenario's cart.js, or check the address, and redirect (303) as the scenario's reference server does.

Data comes from the shared JSON API through httpResource: the listing (every product without its description), the cart and the quick view's product. HttpClient's transfer cache, on by default, writes the server's answers into the page, and httpResource starts from them while the page hydrates, so hydrating asks for nothing.

On the server the shared API sits behind the proxy, at no address the server can reach, so app.config.server.ts provides a server implementation of HttpBackend that answers the same GET requests in-process with the scenario's catalog.js and cart.js, reading the cart cookie from the REQUEST token. The browser uses the default fetch backend.
HttpClient is injected without provideHttpClient(): since Angular 21 it is available by default, with the fetch backend.

The cart is a root service declared with @Service(), Angular 22's shorthand for @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }), shared by the header and the add-to-cart directive. It keeps the cart as an httpResource and sets it to the API's answer after each addition.

The URL's query parameters are the page's state, as on the server: withComponentInputBinding() binds ?q=, ?category=, ?view=, ?subscribed= and ?newsletter= to the page component's inputs, with an input transform for parameters that are absent.

Categories are RouterLinks with [queryParams]: their href loads the category's page without JavaScript, and with it the router navigates in the page. The links have no ?q=, so choosing a category clears the search.

Live search in the browser: each input navigates with router.navigate (queryParamsHandling 'merge', replaceUrl), so ?q= follows the box without a history entry per key, and the list is a computed signal over the listing, with no request and no debounce. The search form stays a GET form for the page without JavaScript.

Quick view keeps its /?view=<id> link, which the server renders with the <dialog> open in the page. Once hydrated, a click loads the product with httpResource and afterRenderEffect calls showModal() once its content has rendered; the URL does not change.
The newsletter's message is a linkedSignal: it starts from ?subscribed= or ?newsletter=invalid, where the server's redirect puts it, and is set to the API's answer (200, or 422 with the reason).
security.allowedHosts in angular.json lists localhost, the host the browser uses through the proxy, so Angular's check of the Host and X-Forwarded-Host headers stays on.
AngularNodeAppEngine trusts the X-Forwarded-For, -Host and -Proto headers the proxy sends. Without it Angular drops them, with a warning on every request.

Scenario rule: /assets/app.css is a plain <link> in src/index.html, and the build has no global stylesheet (styles: []) or component styles, so Angular adds no <style>. Critical CSS inlining, on by default, is turned off with optimization.styles.inlineCritical: it inlines the critical rules of a page's stylesheets and loads the stylesheets themselves asynchronously, and the scenario's stylesheet must stay one plain <link>. Here it found no stylesheet in the build to work on and only warned that it could not read /assets/app.css.
Scenario rule: product images are plain elements with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding, rather than NgOptimizedImage.

The shared modules are imported from ../../scenario with allowJs, so TypeScript reads their JSDoc types. The browser code imports only markup.js; catalog.js and cart.js, which carry the product data, reach the server bundle only.
The CLI's usage analytics are off for the project (cli.analytics: false in angular.json), so builds never ask or report.

stacks.name: Astro + Preact
stacks.summary: Astro renders the page on demand with its Node adapter. The header, the catalog, the quick view and the newsletter are Preact islands, each hydrated when it is needed; they share state through nanostores and call Astro Actions, which the same forms also use without JavaScript.

idioms.choice: output: 'server': the page is rendered on demand for every request, since its header reads the cart cookie. HTML streaming stays on, the default.
The Node adapter in standalone mode. The start command runs its built server, node ./dist/server/entry.mjs, which reads HOST and PORT and also serves the built client files.

Astro components render everything static (the document, the header's brand, the introduction, the footer) with no JavaScript. Four Preact islands hold the interactive parts: the cart summary, the catalog, the quick view and the newsletter.

The cart summary and the catalog (search, categories, result count and cards, one island because they share the filters) hydrate with client:load: they are on the first screen and must respond at once.
The quick view dialog hydrates with client:idle: it is closed until someone asks for it, and a request made before it hydrates waits in its store.
The newsletter, below the 50 cards, hydrates with client:visible. Until then its form still posts without JavaScript.

Islands share state through nanostores and @nanostores/preact: $cart (set by add to cart, read by the header) and $quickView (set by the catalog, read by the dialog). Only the browser writes to the stores; server renders use props.
The page reads the cart cookie and the URL on the server and passes islands their data as props: the cart summary, and the 50 products without descriptions for the catalog.

Search and category filters run in the browser, in the catalog island's state, over the products it received as props: results change on every key without a request, so there is no debounce. The island already holds the listing, so asking the server on each key would only add a request and the scenario's 200 ms wait. Without JavaScript, the GET form and the category links render the filtered page on the server, as in the reference.

Astro Actions instead of the shared JSON API: addToCart and newsletter accept form data, getProduct takes JSON for the quick view, and the islands call them through the actions client. The cart cookie is written with context.cookies in the scenario's format.

The forms work without JavaScript: method=post, with the action's query string (?_action=…) as their action, so the server runs the same action and renders the page. Once hydrated, the islands call the action instead of submitting.
An add to cart posted without JavaScript redirects (303) back to the page it came from on success, so reloading does not add the item again (POST/Redirect/GET).
A newsletter form posted without JavaScript is answered with the page rendered from the action's result, Astro's default for form actions.
The newsletter action validates the address with Zod, using the scenario's rule and message, and both the page and the island show that field's message with isInputError().

security.allowedDomains trusts the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host for https://localhost on any port, so Astro.url is the address the browser uses and the origin check on form posts and actions, on by default, stays on.

Scenario rule: /assets/app.css is linked with a plain <link> in the layout's <head>, the documented way to load a static stylesheet, with no component styles or CSS imports. Astro adds only its 62-byte inline style for <astro-island>.

Scenario rule: card and dialog images are plain elements, the framework's own image syntax inside Preact components, with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding. Astro's would re-encode the shared images and cannot be used inside framework components.
Defaults kept: no <ClientRouter /> and no prefetching, both opt-in. The site is one page, and its filters run in place.

stacks.name: CycleWire
stacks.summary: The reference page activated by CycleWire, built from this repository's source, so every run measures the commit it runs on: the core loads up front, and each interaction's code loads when someone reaches for it. Nothing hydrates.

idioms.choice: The core loads as a module in <head>, with a modulepreload link, as the performance guide recommends.
Vite bundles the page's script, and fromGlob(import.meta.glob(...)) registers every other action as its own chunk. Vite preloads a chunk's dependencies when it is imported.

The server writes the entry's <script> and <link rel="modulepreload"> tags from Vite's manifest, and the modulepreload polyfill is turned off rather than imported, as the backend integration guide allows. Preloading an action's imports stays on.

Add to cart, the action most visitors use first, is imported into the entry and registered from there, so it arrives with the page in the same file, and a tap on it right after the page appears waits only for the server. Everything else loads on intent, the default, and on touch screens also once the page is idle.
The cart shows in one place, the header, so the cart action writes the new count and total into it, on the core alone: the modules guide keeps cyclewire/signals for state that several places show.
The quick view fetches JSON and renders it with cyclewire/dom, which arrives with that action.
The quick view link names its data with cw-prefetch, and the prefetch plugin fetches it on intent, next to the action's code; the action's ctx.fetch() takes that response.

stacks.name: CycleWire, inline
stacks.summary: The CycleWire app with the core inlined in the page: CycleWire starts while the page is still parsing, and each action's code loads as one module when someone reaches for it.

variant.differs: The core is the classic-script build inlined in <head>, which starts from a JSON block that maps actions to URLs, instead of a module loaded with the page; the actions are one module each (esbuild) instead of Vite chunks. It tests the performance guide's advice to inline the core for the fastest activation.

idioms.choice: The core is the classic-script build, inlined in <head> after a <script type="application/json" data-cyclewire> block that maps each action to its module's URL, as the performance guide suggests for the fastest activation: it starts while the page is still parsing, with no request of its own.
Actions are registered by URL from the JSON block, the way a page without a bundler registers them.
esbuild builds each action into one module with what it imports bundled in, so loading an action is one request.

Add to cart, the action most visitors use first, is preloaded with the page: the server writes <link rel="modulepreload"> for its chunk and the chunks it imports, from Vite's manifest, so a tap on it right after the page appears waits only for the server. Everything else loads on intent, the default, and on touch screens also once the page is idle.
The cart shows in one place, the header, so the cart action writes the new count and total into it, on the core alone: the modules guide keeps cyclewire/signals for state that several places show.
The quick view fetches JSON and renders it with cyclewire/dom, which arrives with that action.

The prefetch plugin is a module that registers with the running CycleWire through CycleWire.use(): the quick view link names its data with cw-prefetch, fetched on intent next to the action's code, and ctx.fetch() takes the response. A quick view before that module runs asks the server itself.

stacks.name: CycleWire, intent only
stacks.summary: The CycleWire app with nothing fetched ahead of intent: the core loads up front, and every action's code when someone reaches for it, Add to cart included, on touch screens too.

variant.differs: No <link rel="modulepreload"> for Add to cart, and start({ preload: 'intent' }), which turns off the look-ahead that fetches the code of the actions in view on touch screens. It shows what the two save an interaction, and what they cost a load.

idioms.choice: The core loads as a module in <head>, with a modulepreload link, as the performance guide recommends.
Vite bundles the page's script, and fromGlob(import.meta.glob('./actions/*.js')) registers every action as its own chunk. Vite preloads a chunk's dependencies when it is imported.

The server writes the entry's <script> and <link rel="modulepreload"> tags from Vite's manifest, and the modulepreload polyfill is turned off rather than imported, as the backend integration guide allows. Preloading an action's imports stays on.
The cart shows in one place, the header, so the cart action writes the new count and total into it, on the core alone: the modules guide keeps cyclewire/signals for state that several places show.
The quick view fetches JSON and renders it with cyclewire/dom, which arrives with that action.
The quick view link names its data with cw-prefetch, and the prefetch plugin fetches it on intent, next to the action's code; the action's ctx.fetch() takes that response.

start({ preload: 'intent' }) fetches an action's code only on intent, on every screen: the look-ahead that the default ('auto') runs on touch screens, fetching the code of the actions in view once the page is idle, is off. The server writes <link rel="modulepreload"> for the entry and its imports only.
The build and the actions are the CycleWire app's: this folder has its own entry, which imports ../cyclewire/src/actions/*.js, and resolve.dedupe keeps one copy of cyclewire.

stacks.name: CycleWire, requests from markup
stacks.summary: The CycleWire app with its interactions declared in markup with cyclewire/request, the way htmx builds them: links and forms fetch HTML fragments from the server and swap them in (the results, the header's cart summary, the quick view, the newsletter message), and <cw-stream> messages in an answer update the other parts of the page. The core loads up front, and the request action's code with the page.

variant.differs: Every interaction is cyclewire/request in the page's markup instead of a hand-written action: links and forms fetch HTML fragments from the server and swap them in, <cw-stream> messages in an answer update the rest of the page, and only the quick view has a small action of its own, to open the dialog once the request has filled it. It shows what CycleWire costs, and how fast it is, used the way htmx is.

idioms.choice: The core loads as a module in <head>, with a modulepreload link, as the performance guide recommends.

cyclewire/request is registered once, as the action "request", and the page's forms and links run it with cw-action="request" and a cw-target: each asks the server for HTML and swaps it in, with no JavaScript of the app's own but the quick view's.
Vite bundles the page's script: cyclewire/request, with the morph and message code it brings, is in the entry, and the quick view action, registered as a loader function, is a chunk of its own.

The server writes the entry's <script> and <link rel="modulepreload"> tags from Vite's manifest, and the modulepreload polyfill is turned off rather than imported, as the backend integration guide allows. Preloading an action's imports stays on.

Add to cart, the action most visitors use first, runs cyclewire/request, so request is imported into the entry and registered from there: it arrives with the page in the same file, and a tap on Add to cart right after the page appears waits only for the server. The quick view's action loads on intent, the default, and on touch screens also once the page is idle.

Links request their href and forms their action, so each works without JavaScript through a full page load. The server tells the request action's fetches (Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty) from navigations and answers them with only the part the interaction needs, with Vary: Sec-Fetch-Dest.

Search as you type sits on the search form, so the query goes with the category's hidden field: cw-on-input="request" with cw-debounce="200" (the scenario's 200 ms; the docs' example uses 150), next to cw-action="request" for a submit, which waits out the same debounce. Input runs in restart mode, so each key aborts the request before it. Only the results are swapped, never the input.

The result count, and after a category link the search form's fields and the category links, come in the same answer as <cw-stream> messages, the request action's counterpart to htmx's out-of-band swaps. The category links are morphed, so the link that was tapped keeps focus.
Add to cart swaps the new count and total into the header's cart summary (cw-target=".cart"), so the header needs no store and cyclewire/signals is not used.
The newsletter's answer goes into #newsletter-status. An invalid address is answered with 422, a form sent back with its errors, which the request action shows like any answer.
The quick view link has an empty cw-prefetch: the prefetch plugin fetches the link's own URL on intent, next to the action's code, and the request takes that response.

The quick view runs a small action of the app's own, which runs cyclewire/request and then opens the dialog with showModal(): markup cannot open a modal once the answer is in. The platform's way, an Invoker Command (command="show-modal"), would open it before the product arrives, and needs a button where the page has a link that works without JavaScript.

stacks.name: Hotwire (Turbo + Stimulus)
stacks.summary: The reference page from a plain Node server, with Turbo and Stimulus. Without JavaScript its links and forms load full pages; with Turbo, category links are Drive visits, the search results and the quick view load as Turbo Frames, add to cart and the newsletter answer with Turbo Streams, and two Stimulus controllers submit the search as you type and open the quick view dialog.

idioms.choice: Turbo and Stimulus are installed from npm and bundled with the page's controllers by esbuild, the bundler Turbo's installation guide names, rather than loaded through an import map, the Stimulus handbook's route for Rails: the npm packages ship no minified build, and an import map would load Turbo, Stimulus and each controller as separate modules. Turbo is imported for its side effects only (import "@hotwired/turbo"), as the guide suggests when the code calls no Turbo function; importing it starts Turbo Drive, Frames and Streams.

Stimulus starts with Application.start() and the two controllers are registered by hand (window.Stimulus, Stimulus.register), as the Stimulus handbook shows for build systems other than Rails', which have no controller autoloading. Their files follow its [identifier]_controller.js naming.
The bundle loads with a <script defer> in <head>, as Turbo's handbook shows for the application's bundle; anywhere else, Turbo Drive would load it again with every page change.

The bundle's file name carries a hash of its content (esbuild's entryNames: '[name]-[hash]', recorded in a manifest the server reads) and its tag has data-turbo-track="reload", so a new bundle makes Turbo Drive load the next page in full rather than merge it into the old one. The shared stylesheet has no version in its URL, so it is not tracked.

esbuild minifies the bundle, which its documentation says is usual in production. Everything else is its default for a browser bundle: an IIFE, which a classic script runs, the esnext target, and legal comments (Turbo's copyright notice) collected at the end.

A plain node:http server, no web framework: Turbo is backend-agnostic, and the server follows the conventions of the Rails integration that the handbook offers as the reference: a stream or a redirect depending on the request's Accept header, a frame or the page depending on its Turbo-Frame header.

The page is the app's own copy of the reference template (views.js): the reference render's hooks add attributes but cannot wrap part of the page, and a frame is a <turbo-frame> element wrapped around its content. The frames have no style of their own, and the page lays out exactly like the reference.

Turbo Drive stays on, its default, for every link and form. A category link is an ordinary Drive visit: Turbo fetches the page the server renders for /?category=…, swaps the body and pushes the URL, so the search box is cleared and the chosen link marked by the same render that serves the page without JavaScript.

Search and category filters run on the server, as they do without JavaScript, rather than in a controller that hides cards in the browser: the Turbo handbook starts from the logic living on the server and the browser dealing only with the HTML it sends. That costs a request per search, after the scenario's 200 ms wait, where filtering in the browser would cost neither.

The result count and the cards are a <turbo-frame id="results">, and the GET search form targets it with data-turbo-frame, which the Drive handbook suggests for GET forms: Turbo replaces only the frame, never the input being typed into, and the category goes along in the form's hidden field. There is no data-turbo-action, so typing neither changes the URL nor adds history entries.

A Stimulus controller on the search form submits it 200 ms after the last input, the scenario's delay, with requestSubmit(), which the handbook names for submitting a form from code: unlike submit(), it fires the submit event that Turbo handles. Enter or the button submit at once and cancel the pending timer, and the controller clears it when it disconnects. A newer search cancels one still in flight, which Turbo's frames do on their own.

Both frames have target="_top", so the add-to-cart forms inside them submit for the page, like the page's other forms, rather than navigate their frame (which would mark the whole frame busy while the post is in flight). Only the search form and the Quick view links, which name a frame, navigate one.

A request with the Turbo-Frame header gets only the frame it names, which the Frames handbook allows ("a full document, or just a fragment containing an updated version of the requested frame"); every other request for the same URL gets the full page, so each URL still works without JavaScript.
Answers that depend on the Turbo-Frame header carry Vary: Turbo-Frame, as the Rails integration gives frame requests their own ETag so that a cache never serves one for the other.

Each Quick view link targets a <turbo-frame> inside the <dialog> with data-turbo-frame, so Turbo loads the product into the dialog in place, from the URL that opens it without JavaScript (/?view=…), and the page's URL does not change.

A Stimulus controller on the <dialog> opens it as a modal with showModal() on turbo:frame-load: Turbo only puts HTML into the page, and the handbook leaves behaviour beyond that to Stimulus. The Close button stays a form with method="dialog", which Turbo leaves to the browser.

Add to cart and the newsletter answer Turbo's form submissions, whose Accept header lists text/vnd.turbo-stream.html, with Turbo Stream update actions for #cart-count and #cart-total, or for #newsletter-status, and answer other clients with the 303 redirect the plain forms use: the handbook's respond_to pattern. A redirect back to the page, which Turbo 8 can render as a morphing page refresh, would take a second request and a render of the whole page.
Everything works without JavaScript first, through the plain links and forms and the server's redirects; Drive, frames and streams are layered on top, as the Streams handbook advises.

A newsletter address the server rejects is answered with 422 and a stream with its message, as Turbo expects of a form submission that fails validation. Chrome logs that 422 in the console; the benchmark's journey sends a valid address.

#cart-count and #cart-total carry data-turbo-permanent, the handbook's own example of a cart counter: streams update them in place, and a page Turbo restores from its cache on Back keeps the current cart instead of the one cached with it.

Turbo's other defaults stay on: the page cache, the progress bar, whose default style Turbo inserts as a 251-byte <style> in <head> (within the scenario's 512 bytes), and prefetching a link 100 ms after the pointer comes to rest on it. On the desktop profile, where the pointer rests 100 ms before pressing, a category or quick view link therefore starts loading as the press begins, about 80 ms before the click, which then uses that request. A tap gives no hover before it, so on the mobile profile nothing is prefetched.

stacks.name: htmx
stacks.summary: The reference page from a plain Node server, with htmx attributes on its links and forms. Without JavaScript they load full pages; with htmx they fetch HTML fragments (the results, the quick view, the cart header, the newsletter message) and swap them in.

idioms.choice: htmx.min.js loads with a plain <script> in <head>, as the installation guide describes. The guide mentions neither defer nor the ESM build for a script tag, so neither is used.

No build step: the app's server serves dist/htmx.min.js from the htmx.org npm package at a content-hashed URL. The guide needs no build system and leaves serving the npm file to the app's own tooling.
A plain node:http server, no web framework: a hypermedia app can use any server-side technology.

Progressive enhancement: each hx-get or hx-post repeats its link's href or its form's action (the docs' other option, hx-boost, swaps the whole body), and the server checks the HX-Request header to answer with a fragment or with the full page.

Answers that depend on HX-Request carry Vary: HX-Request, and htmx.config.historyRestoreAsHxRequest is off (set in a <meta name="htmx-config"> tag), as the caching section requires when HX-Request selects fragments.
htmx.config.reportValidityOfForms is on, which the validation section says to always do, so an invalid field is reported as a native form submission would.

Search follows the Active Search example, with the trigger on the search form so the query goes with the form's category field and Enter searches at once: hx-trigger="submit, input changed delay:200ms". The delay is the scenario's 200 ms; the example uses 500 ms. Only the results are swapped, never the input, and no history entry is pushed, as in the example.
Search and category requests both fill #products and share hx-sync="#products:replace", so a newer one aborts one still in flight. The hx-sync page recommends replace for active search.

Answers that update more than their target carry <hx-partial> swap commands, added in 2.0.11 for responses that update several parts of the page (its example is #cart-count and #cart-total): the result count, the cart header, and after a category link the search form and the category links.
Add to cart is answered with partials only, so the form that posted is left unchanged without hx-swap="none".
The docs' first choice for updating other content is to expand the target, but the reference markup has no element around the result count and the list, so the count is a partial.

Quick view swaps the product into the <dialog> and opens it as a modal with hx-on::after-swap="if (!this.open) this.showModal()": htmx has no dialog attribute, and hx-on is its way to handle an htmx event inline.
Forms sent by htmx get their fragment back directly, without the Post/Redirect/Get that the plain forms keep.
An invalid newsletter address is answered with 200 and the message, which htmx swaps by default, rather than 422 plus a responseHandling rule, the alternative the docs show.

stacks.name: Marko
stacks.summary: The page rendered per request by Marko Run's Node server and resumed in the browser by Marko 6, whose one client bundle holds only the code for what can change. A route handler loads the listing and the cart cookie; search and category are template state that toggles the cards' hidden attribute; the forms post to route handlers and are sent with fetch once the page runs; the quick view is a dialog on ?view=, filled from a JSON route when opened in the page.

idioms.choice: The project is laid out the way `npm init marko -- -t basic` writes it: marko in dependencies and @marko/run in devDependencies, the starter's scripts, tsconfig.json and .gitignore (plus .marko-run/, the route types each build writes), routes in src/routes/ and custom tags in src/tags/, and no Vite config, so Marko Run's defaults apply.

Built with `marko-run build` (the starter's `npm run build`) and started with the starter's start script, `node --enable-source-maps ./dist/index.mjs`. No adapter package is installed, so the build uses the Node-based adapter that ships with @marko/run, whose entry is a standalone Node http server with compression and the static files of dist/public. It listens on PORT and has no host setting, so it listens on every interface, 127.0.0.1 included.

The server's request adapter takes the site's origin from the ORIGIN environment variable, which the runner sets to the proxy's address, so ctx.url and the absolute Location of every redirect use the address the browser uses. Without it (or TRUST_PROXY=1), the origin would come from the Host header, over http.

The document (doctype, a <head> with the title, the viewport and the stylesheet, and <body>) is src/routes/+layout.marko, as in the starter, and the page renders everything inside <body>. The header lives in the page rather than the layout because its cart is state that the page's forms update.

Marko's defaults for rendering: the page is rendered for every request, and nothing is prerendered or cached. In the browser it resumes from the state the server serialized into the page, without re-rendering or hydrating anything.

Marko's defaults for code: the compiler ships only what can change. The page's one client bundle updates the cart, the filters, the quick view and the newsletter message, and holds no template for the header, the cards, the newsletter or the footer. No tag is lazily loaded with `import … with { load }`, which is opt-in.

A GET handler, src/routes/+handler.ts, loads the page's data and passes it on with next(), which renders the page with it as $global.data: the product listing without descriptions, the cart summary from the `cart` cookie, the filters and the quick view's product from the query string (read with the scenario's stateFrom), and the newsletter message. It is all synchronous, so the page has no <await>.

The page's state is <let> tags seeded from $global.data (the search, the category, the cart and the quick view's product), and the visible products are a <const> derived from the search and the category. The listing and the filters, which the browser needs to recompute them, are serialized into the page with the rest of the state.

Every card is rendered, as in the reference, and filtering toggles each card's hidden attribute, the pattern the docs show for switching the visibility of server-rendered content: the browser gets code that updates the attribute and the count, and none that renders cards. Results change on every key without a request, so there is no debounce.

The search box is bound with value:=q, the change handler the docs recommend over syncing an input with onInput. It sits in a GET form that loads the filtered page without JavaScript; in the page, the form's onSubmit handler prevents sending it, since the results already follow the box.

Categories are links to /?category=…, a page load without JavaScript. In the page, each link's onClick handler sets the category and clears the search, and leaves a click with a modifier key (a new tab or window) to the browser. aria-current follows the category.

Add to cart and the newsletter are HTML forms that post to route handlers (+handler.ts files exporting Run.POST) at /cart and /newsletter. They read the field with the form option's validator and redirect with a 303 (Post/Redirect/Get): /cart back to the page it was posted from with ctx.back, /newsletter to /?subscribed=<email> or /?newsletter=invalid. The forms work without JavaScript and before the page resumes.

Once the page runs, each form's async onSubmit handler prevents the submission and sends the same FormData with fetch, as the docs' form example does, asking for JSON. The handlers answer such a request with Response.json instead of a redirect: the new cart summary, or the message, with a 422 for an address they refuse. A successful sign-up also resets the form.

The cart is state in the page, bound to each <add-to-cart> tag with cart:=cart. The tag's controllable <let/cart:=input.cart> takes the cart the server answers with, which updates the header; there is no optimistic update.

The handlers read the cart from the Cookie header with the scenario's readCart and write it with a Set-Cookie header from its cartCookie() (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/): Marko Run hands handlers a standard Request, takes a standard Response, and has no cookie helper.
The app's endpoints are at /cart, /newsletter and /products/<id> rather than under /api/, which the benchmark's proxy sends to the shared server. The page uses none of the shared JSON endpoints.

The URLs the page builds from data (the category and Quick view links, and the quick view's request to /products/$id) come from Run.href, which checks the path, params and search against the app's routes; the client build compiles the call to a template string.

The quick view is a native <dialog id="quick-view"> in a <quick-view> tag. Each Quick view link goes to /?view=<id>, which the server renders with the dialog open, the way it shows without JavaScript. In the page, the link's async onClick handler fetches the product with its description from /products/<id>, a GET handler in routes/products/$id/ that answers with Response.json, and sets it as the dialog's product, bound with product:=.

Given a product in the page, the dialog opens as a modal with showModal() from a <script> effect, which runs once the product is rendered, as the docs advise for a modal dialog: open= renders it open but not modal, which is how a page loaded as /?view=<id> keeps it until it is closed. Its Close button is a <form method="dialog">, and its onClose handler clears the product.
The newsletter's message is state in its own <newsletter-form> tag, seeded with the message the server renders for ?subscribed= or ?newsletter=invalid, since nothing else on the page reads it.

Handlers and tags are TypeScript, as in the starter; the build compiles them without a type check. Marko Run writes route types to .marko-run/routes.d.ts on every build, so $global.data is typed from what the handler passes to next().

The handlers and templates import the scenario's modules (catalog, cart, markup, and stateFrom from render.js) from bench/scenario/ by relative path. Vite bundles them into the server, and the browser bundle takes only the markup helpers its code uses (formatting prices and category names, result counts, query matching), with no product data.

Scenario-forced: the shared stylesheet is a <link> in the layout's <head>, and no template has a <style> block, the docs' way to style a component, which Marko Run would bundle into a CSS file. The build emits no CSS.

stacks.name: Next.js
stacks.summary: App Router Server Components render the page per request from the URL and the cart cookie. Server Actions add to the cart and sign up for the newsletter, typing in the search box updates ?q= for the server to render the results, and the quick view is an intercepted route shown in a modal.

idioms.choice: Built with next build (Turbopack, the default bundler) and served by next start, the Node.js server of the deployment docs. --hostname 127.0.0.1 binds it to the loopback address; the port comes from $PORT, which next start reads.

turbopack.root is bench/, the documented setting when a project imports files from outside its folder: the app imports the shared catalog, cart and markup modules from bench/scenario/. Next.js uses the same root for output file tracing.

Every request renders on the server (dynamic rendering, the default for request-time APIs): the root layout reads the cart cookie with cookies() and the page filters by its searchParams. Cache Components, opt-in in Next.js 16, is not enabled.
The header with the cart is in the root layout, the UI every page shares. Layouts do not render again on navigation, so a filter or a search fetches only the page.

Add to cart is a Server Action passed to <form action> in a Server Component, so the form posts before hydration and without JavaScript, and the server answers with the page. The product id is a hidden input, the reference's markup and the forms guide's alternative to bind().

The action sets the cart cookie with cookies().set(). Setting a cookie makes Next.js render the current route again and send it in the action's response, so it calls neither refresh() nor revalidatePath().

The newsletter form is a Client Component with useActionState and a Server Action that returns the message, as the forms guide shows for messages from the server; before hydration the form posts and the page comes back with the message. The button is disabled while the action is pending, as in the guide.

Live search as the Next.js Learn course teaches it: the query is in the URL, useDebouncedCallback (use-debounce) calls router.replace(), and the page's Server Components render the results. The course waits 300 ms; the scenario sets 200 ms for every stack that searches on the server. The course's Suspense boundary and skeleton around the results are left out (see loading.js below).

The page passes the query and category it read from searchParams to the search box as props, where the course's box reads useSearchParams(): the results are data the page loads, and while the quick view is open the URL is /products/<id> but the list behind it keeps its query. The box follows navigations it did not make, so choosing a category clears it.
The search form is next/form: Enter navigates on the client, and without JavaScript it is a GET form that keeps the selected category in a hidden field.

Category filters are <Link>s to /?category=…, and every link keeps the default prefetching. The routes are dynamic and have no loading.js, so, as the prefetching guide describes, the prefetches of links in view carry no page data, and the page is rendered on click.

No loading.js, although the navigation docs suggest one for dynamic routes. With it, every full page load sends the page behind the loading fallback and reveals it with an inline script, so without JavaScript only the fallback shows, and the first product images, the page's LCP element, would sit inside the boundary. The streaming guide advises keeping LCP elements outside Suspense boundaries and not adding boundaries you don't need; the catalog renders from memory in one pass.

The quick view uses the docs' pattern for modals: an @modal parallel route with the intercepting route (.)products/[id]. A Quick view link to /products/<id> opens the product in a modal over the list, with its own URL; back closes it and forward reopens it. On a full page load, /products/<id> renders the shop with the dialog open, which is how the reference shows a quick view without JavaScript, and @modal/page.js renders nothing, so a navigation to / closes that one.

The modal is a native <dialog id="quick-view"> opened with showModal() in an effect, as in the docs' nextgram example. Its Close button (a method="dialog" form) and Escape close it, and the close event calls router.back().

Scenario-forced: the stylesheet is a plain <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.css"> in the root layout's <head>, not an imported CSS file (the docs' default); the docs note that React's <link rel="stylesheet"> can be used. React adds a preload for it.

Scenario-forced: product images are plain elements with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding, not next/image, which serves resized copies from its image optimizer. React preloads the four eager ones.

stacks.name: Next.js, client filtering
stacks.summary: The Next.js app with the list filtered in the browser: a Client Component gets the catalog from the page, keeps ?category= and ?q= in the URL with the native History API and reads them with useSearchParams(). The cart, the newsletter and the quick view are the next app's.

variant.differs: A category or a search does not render the page again on the server: one Client Component holds the whole catalog, filters it in the browser, and updates the URL with window.history.pushState() and replaceState(), which Next.js syncs with useSearchParams(). It shows what filtering in the browser saves a filter and a search, and what moving the list into a Client Component changes in a load.

idioms.choice: Built with next build (Turbopack, the default bundler) and served by next start, the Node.js server of the deployment docs. --hostname 127.0.0.1 binds it to the loopback address; the port comes from $PORT, which next start reads.

turbopack.root is bench/, the documented setting when a project imports files from outside its folder: the app imports the shared catalog, cart and markup modules from bench/scenario/, and the next app's files from apps/next/. The config is the next app's, re-exported: it works the root out from its own folder, two levels up, the same as from this one. Next.js uses the same root for output file tracing.

The root layout, the Server Actions, the Add to cart and newsletter forms and the quick view's routes, modal and content are the next app's files: this app's route files re-export them, and its components import them, through a jsconfig paths alias, @apps/* for apps/. Their own @/ and @scenario/ imports resolve through the next app's jsconfig, and the build takes next and react from this folder alone. The two pages and the catalog are this app's, since they render the Client Component.

Every request renders on the server (dynamic rendering, the default for request-time APIs): the root layout reads the cart cookie with cookies(). On a dynamically rendered route useSearchParams() holds the request's search params during the server render, so the Client Component renders each URL's state into the HTML with no Suspense boundary, and the page does not read searchParams itself. Cache Components, opt-in in Next.js 16, is not enabled.
The header with the cart is in the root layout, the UI every page shares. A filter or a search changes only the URL, so neither the layout nor the page is rendered again for it.

The search box, the category links, the result count and the product list are one Client Component, to which the page's Server Component passes the catalog as a prop: the id, name, category and price of the 50 products, serialized in the RSC payload. The intro and the newsletter section stay in the Server Component.

The component filters in the browser and keeps its state in the URL with the native History API, as the navigation docs show: a category calls window.history.pushState() with /?category=… and clears the search, and every change in the search box calls window.history.replaceState() with ?q= and the category, with no debounce, since nothing is fetched. It reads the state with useSearchParams(), which Next.js syncs with both, so the list follows without a request, and Back and Forward bring it back.

Category filters are plain <a href="/?category=…"> elements, which Next.js does not prefetch, rather than <Link>s, which would prefetch pages this one never asks the server for: a click calls pushState() unless it opens the link elsewhere (a modifier key, another button), and before hydration or without JavaScript the link navigates. The Quick view links stay <Link>s with the default prefetching, as in the next app.

The search form is a plain GET form to /, the reference's, rather than next/form, which navigates on the client when it is sent: without JavaScript it sends ?q= and the selected category from a hidden field, and with it the results already follow the box, so sending it is prevented. The box is uncontrolled, as in the next app, and shows the query when a category or Back and Forward change it.

While the quick view is open over the shop, the URL is /products/<id>, whose search params are empty: the component keeps the filters of the shop's last URL in state, set during render as React describes for information from previous renders, so the list behind the dialog stays as it was, as the next app's page keeps the props it was rendered with.

On a quick view loaded as a page (app/products/[id]), the route on screen is the product's, and pushState() would keep it, dialog and all, under the shop's URL, for Back to bring back. There a category calls router.push() and a search router.replace() 200 ms after the last key, as the next app's links and search do, and the dialog goes with the route (app/@modal/page.js).

Add to cart is the next app's form, a Server Action passed to <form action> with the product id in a hidden input, here rendered by the Client Component, which imports the action from its 'use server' file. React renders the action's id into the form, so before hydration and without JavaScript the browser posts it, and the server answers with the page.

The action sets the cart cookie with cookies().set(). Setting a cookie makes Next.js render the current route again and send it in the action's response, so it calls neither refresh() nor revalidatePath(). After a filter, the route is rendered for the filtered URL and the list keeps its state.

The newsletter form is the next app's Client Component with useActionState and a Server Action that returns the message, as the forms guide shows for messages from the server; before hydration the form posts and the page comes back with the message. The button is disabled while the action is pending, as in the guide.

No loading.js, although the navigation docs suggest one for dynamic routes. With it, every full page load sends the page behind the loading fallback and reveals it with an inline script, so without JavaScript only the fallback shows, and the first product images, the page's LCP element, would sit inside the boundary. The streaming guide advises keeping LCP elements outside Suspense boundaries and not adding boundaries you don't need; the catalog renders from memory in one pass.

The quick view uses the docs' pattern for modals, with the next app's files: an @modal parallel route with the intercepting route (.)products/[id]. A Quick view link to /products/<id> opens the product in a modal over the list, with its own URL; back closes it and forward reopens it. On a full page load, /products/<id> renders the shop with the dialog open, which is how the reference shows a quick view without JavaScript, and @modal/page.js renders nothing, so a navigation to / closes that one.

The modal is a native <dialog id="quick-view"> opened with showModal() in an effect, as in the docs' nextgram example. Its Close button (a method="dialog" form) and Escape close it, and the close event calls router.back().

Scenario-forced: the stylesheet is a plain <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.css"> in the root layout's <head>, not an imported CSS file (the docs' default); the docs note that React's <link rel="stylesheet"> can be used. React adds a preload for it.

Scenario-forced: product images are plain elements with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding, not next/image, which serves resized copies from its image optimizer. React preloads the four eager ones; since a Client Component renders them, the preloads come in a Link response header, where the next app's Server Components send hints that become tags.

stacks.name: Nuxt
stacks.summary: The page rendered per request by Nuxt's Node server and hydrated by Vue. useFetch loads the products and the cart from Nitro server routes; search and category live in the URL and filter the list in the browser; the forms post to server routes and are sent with $fetch once hydrated; the quick view is a dialog on ?view=, filled with useAsyncData.

idioms.choice: Built with `nuxt build` (the starter's `npm run build`) and started with `node .output/server/index.mjs`, the Node.js server entry of the deployment docs. It reads PORT and HOST (127.0.0.1) from the environment, and runs with NODE_ENV=production, as the docs ask.

The project is laid out the way `npm create nuxt` writes it: Nuxt 4's app/ directory, the starter's nuxt.config.ts (compatibilityDate, devtools), tsconfig.json and scripts, and <NuxtRouteAnnouncer> in app.vue. The starter's generate script and public/ folder are left out: nothing is prerendered, and /favicon.ico is answered by the shared server.

The shop is app/pages/index.vue, shown by <NuxtPage>, with the header and the footer around it in app.vue, where the docs put markup every page shares when there is one layout. The pages directory brings in vue-router, as it would in a shop with more than one page; the docs note that an app made of app.vue alone leaves it out.

Universal rendering, Nuxt's default: the server renders every request and Vue hydrates the page. There are no route rules, so nothing is prerendered or cached, and SSR streaming, an experimental option, is off.

A `#scenario` alias in nuxt.config points at the shared modules in bench/scenario/, and Nuxt passes its aliases on to Nitro. The server routes import the catalog and the cart from them; the Vue app imports only the markup helpers (prices, result counts, query matching), so no product data is bundled for the browser.

The app's endpoints are Nitro server routes in server/routes/ (GET /products, GET /products/<id>, GET and POST /cart, POST /newsletter) rather than server/api/: the benchmark's proxy sends every /api/ path to the shared server, and server/routes/ is where the docs put routes without the /api prefix. The page uses none of the shared JSON endpoints.

Data is loaded with useFetch: the page fetches the product listing (without descriptions), and app.vue the cart, with the key 'cart'. On the server, useFetch calls the routes in-process and forwards the request's cookies, and the results reach the browser in the payload, so hydration fetches nothing.

The server routes read and write the cart cookie with h3's utilities, as the docs show for cookies in server routes: the Cookie header goes to the scenario's readCart, and setCookie writes the name, value and attributes of its cartCookie() (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/). The cookie is HttpOnly, so the page gets the cart from the server rather than from useCookie.

Search and category are query parameters, read with useRoute(). The list is a computed over the listing the page already has, the way Vue's guide shows a filtered list, so a filter change is a client-side navigation with no request, and no debounce.

The search box is a GET form (action="/") that loads the results without JavaScript. With it, every input calls navigateTo with the new ?q= and replace: true, keeping the category, so results update as you type without a history entry per key.

Categories are <NuxtLink>s to /?category=…: a client-side navigation with JavaScript, a page load without it. They leave ?q= out, so choosing a category clears the search. Vue Router marks a link as current by its path and parameters, not its query, so the category and Quick view links set aria-current themselves.

NuxtLink keeps its default prefetching of links in view, which starts once the page is idle: their route's code is already loaded here, and checking whether their pages were prerendered fetches Nuxt's app manifest (/_nuxt/builds/meta/<buildId>.json) once. appManifest is on by default.

navigationRepaint, on by default, is kept: before each client-side navigation (a key typed in the search box, a category, a quick view) the router waits for one animation frame, so the browser can paint first.

Add to cart and the newsletter are HTML forms that post to server routes, which set the cookie or check the address and then redirect with h3's sendRedirect (303 See Other), the docs' way to redirect from a server route, so the forms work without JavaScript and before hydration.

Once the page is hydrated, @submit.prevent sends the same request with $fetch, which the docs recommend for requests made from event handlers. $fetch asks for JSON, so the route answers with the new cart or the message instead of a redirect.

The cart the server answers with is written to the 'cart' data through useNuxtData('cart'), the docs' way to update fetched data after a mutation, so the header updates without another request. The header waits for the server's answer: there is no optimistic update.
An address the server rejects gets a 422 with the scenario's message (setResponseStatus), which the form shows; without JavaScript, the redirect to ?newsletter=invalid shows the same message.

The quick view is a native <dialog id="quick-view">. Each Quick view link is a <NuxtLink> to ?view=<id> that keeps the search and the category, and the dialog's product, with the description the listing leaves out, comes from useAsyncData with a reactive key on that id, which fetches /products/<id> when it changes. Loaded with ?view=<id>, the server renders the dialog open, which is how it shows without JavaScript.

Opened in the page, the dialog is shown with showModal() once its product has arrived, which makes the page behind it inert and lets Escape close it. Closing it (its Close button is a <form method="dialog">) goes back in history when the page opened it, so Back and Forward stay in step with the screen, and otherwise replaces the address with one without ?view=.

Scenario-forced: the shared stylesheet is a <link> in app.head in nuxt.config, the docs' way to include an external stylesheet, next to the title and lang. No component has a <style> block, so the build emits no CSS for the page.
Scenario-forced: product images are plain elements with the reference's attributes, rather than from Nuxt Image, which the performance guide recommends for optimising images.

Code loading keeps Nuxt's defaults: the entry and the chunks the page needs are modulepreloaded, the error pages' chunks are prefetched, and no component is lazy-loaded or lazily hydrated, two optimisations the performance guide suggests considering.

stacks.name: Qwik City
stacks.summary: The page as a Qwik City app on its Node.js server adapter: rendered per request and resumed in the browser, nothing hydrates. Route loaders read the cart cookie and the URL, the forms are route actions, search and filters are signals, and the quick view fetches its product through server$.

idioms.choice: The production server is the one `npm run qwik add node-server` sets up: Node's http.createServer with Qwik City's Node middleware, which renders the page and serves the client build from dist/. It starts with `npm run serve`. The adapter's entry listens on $PORT; it also takes $HOST (127.0.0.1), which the template leaves out.
`npm run build` runs `qwik build`: the client build, the adapter's server build and a type check. The adapter's static generation step prerenders no page, since none is listed for it.
The page is rendered for every request and sets no cacheControl, as the docs advise for pages that differ per visitor: the header shows the visitor's cart.
The Node middleware takes the site's origin from the ORIGIN environment variable (the runner sets it to the proxy's address), and its CSRF check compares form posts' Origin header with it.

Code loading keeps Qwik's defaults: the page resumes instead of hydrating, the Qwik Loader is a module script, and the preloader adds <link rel="modulepreload"> for the bundles the page's listeners may need.

No service worker. Since Qwik 1.14 the preloader has replaced the prefetching service worker; <ServiceWorkerRegister /> stays only in older apps, to unregister it, and the 1.20 starter has neither it nor a service-worker.ts.

Two routeLoader$s in the route file: the cart summary, read from the cart cookie with Qwik City's cookie API, and the catalog (every product without its description, with the search, category and ?view= product from the URL). The page passes their values to its components as props.

Add to cart and the newsletter are routeAction$s used through <Form>: without JavaScript it posts natively, with it Qwik City submits it with fetch and runs the route loaders again, which updates the header's cart.

The actions validate with the scenario's own functions (readCart, add, validEmail) and return failures with fail(): 404 for an unknown product, 422 for a rejected address, with the scenario's message. There is no zod$ schema.

The cart cookie is set with Qwik City's cookie API, with the same name, value and attributes as the scenario's cartCookie(). Its value is live within the request, so the loaders that run after the action read the new cart.

Search and category filters work in the browser: the query (bound with bind:value) and the category are signals, and the list is a useComputed$ over the loader's products, so results change as you type without a request, and without the 200 ms debounce that asking the server would need.

The search form keeps action="/" method="get" and each category is a link to /?category=, so without JavaScript both load the page. With it, preventdefault:submit and preventdefault:click keep the page, and a category's onClick$ sets it and clears the search.
The list is rendered with .map() and a key per product. Each card is a component with primitive props, so a filter change renders only the cards it adds.
The brand link is a plain <a>, a full page load, rather than <Link>: the docs note that full page loads are cheap in Qwik, and the page has no other route.
Quick view asks for the product's details with a server$ function, Qwik City's RPC. Its link's href, ?view=, renders the dialog open on the server without JavaScript.

The <dialog id="quick-view"> opens with showModal() from a useVisibleTask$, the task that runs after rendering, so the modal never shows before its content. The component that holds it only mounts once a product is chosen, so nothing runs eagerly on page load.

Scenario: the shared stylesheet is a plain <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.css"> in root.tsx instead of the starter's imported global.css, with no component styles. The only inline <style> is Qwik City's own :root{view-transition-name:none}.
Scenario: plain elements with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding, instead of Qwik's image optimization.
The title comes from the route's head export. RouterHead renders it with the viewport meta, without the starter's canonical link and favicon.
The shared modules are imported from ../../scenario. For `npm run dev`, server.fs.allow lets Vite's dev server serve that folder; production builds need no setting.

stacks.name: SolidStart
stacks.summary: The page rendered per request by SolidStart 2 on Nitro's Node server and hydrated by Solid. Queries whose bodies run on the server load the products and the cart; search and category live in the URL and filter the list in the browser; the forms post to server actions and are sent by the router once hydrated, with the new cart in the same response; the quick view is a dialog on ?view=.

idioms.choice: The project is laid out the way `npm init solid` writes it for SolidStart 2 (the basic template): vite.config.ts with solidStart() and nitro(), src/app.tsx with the router, the file routes, a MetaProvider and a Suspense boundary, and the template's entry-client.tsx, entry-server.tsx, tsconfig.json and scripts. Its dependency ranges are pinned to what they install: SolidStart 2.0.5, Solid 1.9.15, Solid Router 1.0.0, Vite 8.3.1 and Nitro 3.0.260610-beta, the Nitro that SolidStart 2.0.5 is tested with. The template's public/ folder and its icon link are left out: /favicon.ico is answered by the shared server.

Built with `vite build` (the starter's `npm run build`) and started with `node .output/server/index.mjs` (its `npm start`): nitro() after solidStart(), as the deployment guide shows, with Nitro's default node_server preset. The server reads PORT and HOST (127.0.0.1) from the environment. SolidStart 2 asks for Node.js 24 or newer.
Server rendering on every request, SolidStart's default (ssr: true), in its default streaming mode. Nothing is prerendered (no Nitro prerender routes) and nothing is cached.

A `#scenario` alias (resolve.alias in vite.config.ts) points at the shared modules in bench/scenario/. The server functions import the catalog and the cart from them; the components import only the markup helpers (prices, result counts, query matching), so no product data is bundled for the browser. server.fs.allow lets the dev server serve them.

The shop is src/routes/index.tsx, a file route, with the header (and its cart) and the footer in the router's root, which every page shares. The starter's catch-all [...404].tsx route stays, so an unknown address answers 404.

Data is loaded with Solid Router's query and createAsync, with "use server" inside each query so that its body runs only on the server: the product listing (without descriptions), the cart from the `cart` cookie, and the quick view's product. While the page renders they run in-process, and their results reach the browser with the page, so hydration fetches nothing.

The route exports route.preload, which starts its queries before it renders, as the data-fetching guide shows. The router also runs it when a link to the page is hovered (after 20 ms) or touched, its default, so a Quick view link starts loading its product before the click.

The page's data is read with deferStream: true, the documented way to keep data out of streaming when it must be in the first HTML: the page has to be complete without JavaScript, and streamed sections are put in place by a script. With the data in memory the HTML is the same either way.

Search and category are search parameters, read with useSearchParams. The list is a memo over the listing the page already has, so a filter change is a client-side navigation with no request, and no debounce.

The search box is a GET form (action="/") that loads the results without JavaScript. With it, every input calls setSearchParams with the new query and replace: true, which keeps the category and adds no history entry per key; submitting would only show what is already shown, so the submit is prevented.

Categories are plain links to /?category=…, which the router follows in the page and which load the page without JavaScript (the docs plan to deprecate the A component in favour of native links). They leave ?q= out, so choosing a category clears the search, and the current one has aria-current.

Add to cart and the newsletter are Solid Router actions whose bodies run on the server ("use server"), passed to <form action={…} method="post">. The form's action attribute is the server function's address (/_server?id=…), so without JavaScript, or before hydration, the browser posts the form there and SolidStart redirects back to the page it came from; once hydrated, the router sends the same form with fetch. The product id is a hidden input, as in the reference markup.

There are no /cart or /newsletter endpoints: the docs prefer queries and actions to an API route for data that only the page's UI needs. (The benchmark's proxy sends /api/ to the shared server; the page uses none of the shared JSON endpoints.)

Add to cart returns reload({ revalidate: getCart.key }): only the cart changed, so only the cart query is revalidated, rather than every query on the page (the default after an action), which would also send the whole listing again.

Single-flight mutations, the router's default, are kept: after the action, SolidStart renders the revalidated cart query on the server and sends it in the action's own response, so the header updates without a second request. The header waits for that response: there is no optimistic update.

The newsletter action returns json({ message }, { revalidate: [] }), with the scenario's message for a valid or a rejected address, and the page shows it with useSubmission(subscribe).result; nothing needs revalidating. Without JavaScript, SolidStart carries the result in a short-lived `flash` cookie on its redirect, and the server renders the same message from it.

The cart cookie is written with setCookie from @solidjs/start/http in the shared format (URL-encoded JSON, Path=/, SameSite=Lax, HttpOnly), and read from the Cookie header of getRequestEvent().request with the scenario's readCart. Reading it from the request event matters for single flight: the re-render after an action runs with a request that carries the cookie the action has just set, while the @solidjs/start/http helpers read the original request.

The quick view is a native <dialog id="quick-view">. Each Quick view link is a plain link to ?view=<id> that keeps the search and the category, with noScroll so that the page stays where it is; the dialog's product, with the description the listing leaves out, comes from a query on that id. Loaded with ?view=<id>, the server renders the dialog open, which is how it shows without JavaScript.

Opened in the page, the dialog is shown with showModal() once its product has arrived, which makes the page behind it inert and lets Escape close it. Closing it (its Close button is a <form method="dialog">) goes back with navigate(-1) when the page opened it, so Back and Forward stay in step with the screen, and otherwise replaces the address with one without ?view=.
The title is set with @solidjs/meta's <Title> in the router's root, where the docs put the MetaProvider; lang is on the document's <html>.
Scenario-forced: the shared stylesheet is a plain <link> in the document of entry-server.tsx rather than a CSS import, the docs' way to style components; no component imports CSS.
Scenario-forced: product images are plain elements with the reference's attributes, referred to by absolute path as the docs show for public assets.

Workaround: SolidStart 2.0.5 imports its development toolbar into the error boundary it also renders in production. The toolbar is left out of production builds, as the docs say, but the stylesheets its modules import are side effects the bundler keeps, so every page would link a 17 kB stylesheet of toolbar styles (and load 1.9 kB of module-level script from the toolbar's UI library). A small plugin in vite.config.ts declares the toolbar module free of side effects in builds, so the bundler drops it with its stylesheets, as the one-stylesheet rule requires.

stacks.name: SvelteKit
stacks.summary: The page rendered per request by SvelteKit's Node adapter and hydrated by Svelte 5. Search and category live in the URL and filter the list in the browser; add to cart and the newsletter are form actions enhanced with use:enhance; the quick view is a shallow-routed modal.

idioms.choice: adapter-node builds a standalone Node server: `vite build`, then `node build`, which reads PORT, HOST and ORIGIN from the environment.

The project is laid out the way `npx sv create` writes it: SvelteKit's options passed to its Vite plugin in vite.config.js (with runes mode on) and the template's src/app.html, with adapter-node in place of adapter-auto.
A `$scenario` alias points at the shared scenario modules outside the app's folder, which the server imports rather than copying; Vite's server.fs.allow lets the dev server read them.

One +page.server.js load returns the cart from the `cart` cookie, the product listing and the quick view's product. It reads only the `view` search parameter: SvelteKit tracks search parameters one by one, so changing the search or the category does not run it again.

Search and category are search parameters in the URL, where the docs keep filters that affect server rendering. Categories are plain links, so choosing one clears the search. The page reads both from page.url and filters the products it already has with $derived, so a filter change is a client-side navigation with no request.

The search box is a GET form, which the router handles like a link. It is sent on every input (requestSubmit) with data-sveltekit-keepfocus, -noscroll and -replacestate, so results update as you type without a history entry per key. Filtering in the browser needs no debounce.

Add to cart and the newsletter are named form actions (?/add and ?/subscribe), so they work without JavaScript. Form actions are the stable API; the form remote function the docs point to as their successor is still experimental.
Both forms use use:enhance with its defaults: it posts with fetch and, after a success, resets the form and re-runs the page's load (invalidateAll), which reads the cart cookie the action set.

The cart cookie is written with SvelteKit's cookies API (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Secure by default) in the shared format, and read with cookies.get, which also sees a cookie set earlier in the same request, so a post without JavaScript renders the new cart.
An invalid email returns fail(422) with the message, which the page shows through the form prop, with or without JavaScript.

The quick view uses shallow routing, as the docs show for a modal: the link's click handler awaits preloadData (already started by data-sveltekit-preload-data on hover or tap), then calls pushState, and the dialog opens with showModal(); Back closes it. The link's address, /?view=<id>, is the fallback: the server renders it with the dialog open.
Add to cart inside the quick view calls refreshAll after the action instead of use:enhance's default invalidateAll, which also resets page.state and would close the dialog.
data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover" on <body>, as in the default template: a link's data starts loading when the pointer rests on it or a finger touches it.
The shared stylesheet is a plain <link> in src/app.html, and no component has a <style> block, as the scenario requires.
Images are plain elements with the reference's attributes, as the scenario requires, rather than the @sveltejs/enhanced-img the docs suggest for build-time optimisation.
